clock_dir_to: Subtractive clock connective: the hour, then "minus", then the fraction or
the minutes.  Same Arabic borrowing as ar/clock_dir_to.voc ("إلا").
"ɣir" is the standard spelling.  @athmanemokraoui, a native Kabyle speaker,
answering on https://github.com/TigreGotico/chronologia/pull/846#issuecomment-5573978767:
"Minus on the clock is 'ɣir' -- standard INALCO Kabyle orthography does
not use macrons or dots on standard vowels/liquids for this loan."
"ɣiṛ" is the underdotted variant the Kabyle sentences on Tatoeba write
(native contributors), with their English pairs:
"Ha-tt-an d ttmanya ɣiṛ ṛṛbeɛ."  -- "It's a quarter to eight."
"Ha-tt-an d lweḥda ɣiṛ ṛṛbeɛ."   -- "It's a quarter to one."
"Ha-tt-an d ssaɛtin ɣiṛ ṛṛbeɛ."  -- "It's quarter to two."
"Ha-tt-an d tmenya ɣir ɛecra."   -- "It's ten to eight."
The two sources disagree on the underdot and both surfaces stay readable:
a parser accepts every attested variation, and someone will type this one.
The standard form to WRITE is "ɣir" above.  The last pair also shows the
slot after the connective takes plain minutes, not only the quarter -- a
reading @athmanemokraoui confirms ("d lɛecṛa ɣiṛ xemsa" for five to ten,
answer 7 of the same comment).
clock_fraction_15: "ṛṛbeɛ" = the quarter, the Arabic-borrowed fraction Kabyle uses on the clock.
The two spellings are conditioned variants of one word, not a right and a
wrong one.  @athmanemokraoui, native Kabyle speaker, on
"'ṛbeɛ' after a vowel (u ṛbeɛ), 'ṛṛbeɛ' with the assimilated article
(ɣir ṛṛbeɛ).  The emphatic ṛ requires the underdot."
The Kabyle sentences on Tatoeba (native contributors) write both, and he
confirms the additive quarter reading ("d lɛecṛa u ṛbeɛ", answer 8):
"Ha-tt-an d leḥḍac u ṛṛbeɛ."   -- "It's a quarter past eleven."
"Ha-tt-an d ttnac u ṛṛbeɛ."    -- "It's a quarter past twelve."
"Ha-tt-an d tesɛa u ṛbeɛ."     -- "It's quarter past nine."
"Ha-tt-an d ttmanya ɣiṛ ṛṛbeɛ." -- "It's a quarter to eight."
The dotless "rrbeɛ" is the plain-ASCII fallback a keyboard without the
emphatic produces; it parses, but the emphatic ṛ above is the spelling.
clock_fraction_30: "azgen" = half; in the construct state after the connective "d" it surfaces
"ɣef ṛṛebɛa d wezgen n tmeddit"   (half past four in the evening)
"ɣef leḥdac d wezgen n tṣ̣ebḥit"  (half past eleven in the morning)
Tatoeba Kabyle also writes the construct-state "uzgen" after the connective:
"Attan qrib d lweḥda d uzgen." -- "It's almost half past one already."

clock_meridiem_pm: Kabyle pm surfaces.
"n tmeddit" is CLDR 47's dayPeriods pm for kab (cldr-dates-full/main/kab/
ca-gregorian.json) and is how kab.wikipedia writes a pm clock reading:
"Deg wass-nni, ɣef 4:40 n tmeddit, yiwet n terbaεt n yisafagen ..." (Bgayet)
"azal n 12:30 n tmeddit, takarust n Meɛṭub tettwaḥbes" (Lwennas Meɛṭub)
"ɣef lxemsa n tmeddit, anmahal n Ldzayer deg Fṛansa yemlal ..."
(Tafsut n Yimaziɣen)
"uzal" is the broad-daylight noun; on the clock it closes a midday reading.
The genitive "n uzal" is the standard form.  @athmanemokraoui, native Kabyle
speaker, on
https://github.com/TigreGotico/chronologia/pull/846#issuecomment-5573978767:
"'D ttnac n uzal' is the grammatically correct and standard form (genitive
n + annexed state uzal).  'D ttnac uzal' is only an informal elision in
rapid speech."
The bare apposition is what Tatoeba writes -- "Tella qrib d ttnac uzal."
("It was nearly noon.") -- and it stays readable: an informal register is
still Kabyle a speaker says.  The form to write is "n uzal" above.

marker_at: The Kabyle preposition that opens a clock reading.  kab.wikipedia writes
every spoken clock time in Tafsut n Yimaziɣen with "ɣef":
"ɣef lweḥda n tṣ̣ebḥit", "ɣef tlata n tmeddit", "ɣef tmanya n tmeddit"
"d" is the predicative copula ("it is ..."), the ordinary way to ANSWER the
question "what time is it": "d lxemsa n tmeddit" = "it is five in the
evening".  It is the same particle as marker_and.voc / clock_dir_past.voc;
the two readings are kept apart by position, since the copula only ever
opens the phrase and the conjunction only ever stands between an hour and
